t: Describe the Painting -- Sweeping Mixed Color Sums Across a Number Line
o: Each segment paints the half-closed interval [start, end) with a unique color; where segments overlap, the visible color is the set of all active colors and only the sum of that set is reported. We must output the fewest non-overlapping half-closed segments reproducing the painting. Example 1, [[1,4,5],[4,7,7],[1,7,9]], gives [1,4) the set {5,9} (sum 14) and [4,7) the set {7,9} (sum 16), so the answer is [[1,4,14],[4,7,16]]. Example 3, [[1,4,5],[1,4,7],[4,7,1],[4,7,11]], exposes the key subtlety: both halves have sum 12, yet the color sets {5,7} and {1,11} differ, so the output must stay [[1,4,12],[4,7,12]] and never merge into a single segment [1,7]. Coordinates are at most 100000 and with up to 2*10^4 segments of color up to 10^9, sums reach about 2*10^13 -- 64-bit arithmetic is mandatory in C++/Java.
k: Record +color at every segment start and -color at every end; sweeping coordinates in order keeps a running total equal to the mixed-color sum at the current position.
An output segment must break at every coordinate where some input segment starts or ends -- even when the net sum change is zero, because the underlying color set changes.
Since all colors are distinct, equal neighboring sums always mean different color sets, so adjacent pieces must never be merged merely because their sums match.

a.n: Approach 1: Paint Unit Cells With Boundary Markers
a.i: Simulate the painting literally: keep a difference array over the number line plus a marker at every coordinate where any segment starts or ends. Walk cell by cell, applying the pending delta only at marked boundaries (which forces a piece break), and stretch the current output piece while the running mix stays positive and untouched.
s: Build a delta array (+color at start, -color at end) and a boolean boundary array from the segments.
Scan positions left to right; at each boundary apply the delta to the running sum and force a new piece.
While the running sum is positive with no intervening boundary, extend the last output piece by one cell.
Unpainted stretches (running sum 0) end the current piece; return the collected pieces.
a.t: O(n + L) -- one pass over segments plus one pass over the number line up to L = max end coordinate
a.sp: O(L) -- delta and boundary arrays sized by the largest coordinate (L <= 10^5)

a.n: Approach 2: Coordinate Sweep With a Sorted Event Map
a.i: Compress coordinates into a map from position to net color delta, then visit its keys in increasing order. Between consecutive event positions the mix sum is constant, so each visited interval [prev, pos) with positive sum becomes one output segment. The event map naturally breaks pieces at every genuine boundary -- including net-zero swaps like {5,7} becoming {1,11} -- because those coordinates exist as keys.
s: Accumulate +color at each start and -color at each end in a sorted map.
Iterate positions in increasing order, remembering the previous position and current sum.
If the interval [prev, pos) carries a positive sum, append [prev, pos, sum] to the result.
Add the delta at pos and continue to the next interval.
a.t: O(n log n) -- inserting into a balanced map and sorting at most 2n event coordinates dominate
a.sp: O(n) -- the event map stores at most 2n distinct positions

w: Present the event-map sweep in an interview -- it is shorter, independent of the coordinate range, and generalizes to huge inputs. The classic mistake is merging adjacent pieces with equal sums: Example 3 proves equal sums can hide different color sets, so pieces must break at every input endpoint. Beware 32-bit overflow in C++/Java (sums reach 2*10^13), and remember half-closed [a, b) semantics release a color exactly at coordinate end. Natural follow-up: report the actual color sets, which the same sweep supports by maintaining a multiset of active colors.
